title: Hancock Oil Co. v. Independent Distributing Co. (1944)
summary: Interpleader could address rival demands for the same royalties without the older rigid requirement of a common source of title.
notes:
This is a state interpleader decision. Federal rule interpleader and statutory interpleader have separate jurisdiction and service requirements.

The Hopkinses leased land to Hancock Oil and Bush Oil in 1936; Independent Distributing later claimed the Hopkinses held the land in trust for it and demanded the $1,500 in accrued landowner royalties; the California Supreme Court held that the lessee's contractual obligation to pay rent is not an 'independent liability' barring interpleader and that the rule against a tenant disputing the landlord's title does not prevent the tenant from interpleading rival claimants.

sections.Parties: Hancock Oil was the stakeholder facing claims by the parties asserting entitlement to royalties under the oil arrangement.
sections.Material Facts: One claimant relied on the lease and its ownership relationship; another asserted an interest through a trust or competing entitlement. Hancock faced conflicting demands concerning the same royalty payments. The controversy raised older restrictions on interpleader, including whether claimants’ titles derived from a common source and whether the stakeholder owed an independent obligation to one claimant.
sections.Procedural History: The California court examined the availability of interpleader under the revised statutory procedure and accepted its use for the competing demands described.
sections.Issue: Did the different grounds asserted by the rival claimants prevent interpleader of the royalty dispute?
sections.Holding: No. The procedure could determine entitlement to the disputed obligation under the broader statutory approach.
sections.Reasoning: Interpleader protects a stakeholder from the risk of paying the same obligation twice when rival claimants assert inconsistent entitlement. Older formal limitations were not treated as controlling where the statutory procedure had broadened access. That rationale still requires attention to the underlying obligation: genuinely independent liabilities cannot be extinguished merely by describing them as competing demands for one fund.

learning.why: Interpleader could address rival demands for the same royalties without the older rigid requirement of a common source of title.

topics.cp-interpleader: Competing demands for the same royalty obligation created a stakeholder problem. The court distinguished rival claims to one obligation from independent liabilities that cannot be collapsed into a single fund.
topics.cp-frcp-22: The California decision tracks the liberalization of interpleader later embodied in Rule 22, which abandons the common-source and independent-liability limits.
